lead: Start, sail the course, finish: each word has a definition. Here are the string test, the marks, the finish and flags S, N, C and M.

sections.title: A string pulled taut past every mark
refs: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course
RRS 28.1, RRS definition Sail the Course

blocks.p: Rule 28.1: **sail the course** in the sailing instructions, whatever the leader does. Picture a string along your track from your approach to the starting line until you finish. Pulled taut, it passes each mark on its required side and in order, touches each rounding mark, and passes between the marks of a **gate** from the direction of the previous mark; then you may round either gate mark.

fig.note: Outside the gate: the string never passed between the marks

blocks.p: A **mark** is an object the instructions tell you to leave on a stated side, or a committee vessel at the end of a starting or finishing line. Only marks that begin, bound or end your leg have a required side.
A boat that did not sail the course is scored **NSC** without a hearing. If the committee is wrong, request redress.

sections.title: Unwind it before you finish
refs: RRS 28.2, RRS definition Sail the Course

blocks.p: Rule 28.2 lets you correct any error in sailing the course until you finish. A mark left on the wrong side is **unwound**, so that the taut string lies on the required side. Circling the mark once does not do it; neither do penalty turns.

fig.note: Marks to port; this one was left to starboard

list: Sail back past the mark on the side you came.
Round it leaving it on the required side.
Carry on: no penalty is owed.

blocks.p: Pushed by another boat, swept by the current or capsized, you still unwind. Sailing back, you keep your ordinary rights. Even after crossing the finishing line you may go back, correct the error and cross again.

While racing you must not touch a starting mark before starting, a mark that begins, bounds or ends your leg, or a finishing mark after finishing. Hull, crew or equipment all count. Anything intentionally attached to a mark is part of it; a committee boat's **anchor line** is not. Both gate marks bound the leg.

fig.note: A sheet, the boom or a hand on it: a touch

head: What happened
What you owe
rows: You touch a mark, even by bad luck
One-Turn Penalty: get well clear, then one tack and one gybe
Another boat's foul forces you onto it
You foul a boat and touch the mark in one incident
A hearing later finds the touch

blocks.p: Rule 31 applies only while you are **racing**: from your preparatory signal until you have finished and cleared the line and marks, and not after a general recall.

sections.title: Hull across the line from the course side

blocks.p: You **finish** when any part of your hull crosses the finishing line from the course side, between its marks. A spinnaker ahead of the bow does not count, and no horn is needed. A committee boat flying a blue flag is in position at the finish. You need not cross completely.

fig.note: The bow is across from the course side: finished

blocks.p: You have not finished if, after crossing, you take a penalty, go back to correct an error or carry on sailing the course. A penalty near the line is taken with the hull wholly on the course side. Until you clear the line and marks you are still racing; after that, or once retired, you must not interfere with boats racing.

head: Rule 35
Result
rows: A boat sails the course and finishes in time
The race counts, even if she is later disqualified
You miss the instructions' finishing window

blocks.p: After the start the committee may **shorten** the course or **abandon** the race for foul weather, too little wind to finish in time, a mark missing or out of position, or another reason affecting safety or fairness; it may also shorten to fit in later races. Once a boat has finished in time it must weigh the consequences for all boats before abandoning.

fig.note: S: two sounds · N: three sounds

blocks.p: S must be shown before the first boat crosses the new line: between a rounding mark and the staff showing S, between the gate marks, or at a line the course makes you cross. Over a class flag a signal is for that class only. After N alone, return to the starting area. Redress needs an improper act of the committee: a late signal is one, a proper abandonment is not.

fig.note: Finish between mark 3 and the boat showing flag S

blocks.p: In a restart or resail earlier breaches are not penalised, except rules 2, 30.2, 30.4 and 69, and rule 14 with injury or serious damage. Only rule 30.4 keeps you out.

The committee may move the **next mark**: flag C with repeated sounds, shown before boats begin the leg; the new mark need not be laid yet. Later legs may then change without signals to keep the course's shape. A signal made in time binds you even if you missed it.

head: With flag C
Meaning
rows: New compass bearing of the leg

blocks.p: A mark **missing or out of position** is put back or replaced by a similar one, without a signal, or by an object showing flag M with repeated sounds, which is then the mark. If that is impossible, the race is abandoned. A mark in position may not be moved mid-leg.

fig.note: Mark 2 has gone: the RIB showing M is now the mark
